true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The client-side limit ignores the configured attachment size

This replaces the type-specific `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` limit with a fixed 10 MB limit for every upload. Sites that configure attachments above 10 MB will now reject otherwise valid files in the browser before they reach the server; sites with lower limits also receive an inaccurate client-side error threshold. Keep the attachment limit configurable while allowing the intended larger image uploads.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Oversized animated GIFs can lose all but their first frame

This passes `allow_animated_thumbnails` to the upload downsize operation, but that setting controls thumbnail generation, not whether an uploaded animation should be preserved. When it is false, `downsize_instructions` uses ImageMagick with `#{from}[0]`, which processes only the first frame. Any oversized animated GIF is therefore replaced by a static image when the tempfile is overwritten, causing irreversible loss of the animation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when no embed category matches

This indexes the first row of an inner join without checking whether the query returned anything. On installations where `embed_category` is unset, blank, or names a category that no longer exists, the result is empty and this raises before the migration can complete, blocking upgrades. Handle the missing match and fall back to the uncategorized category.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.

The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.

false_positives.candidate:
Configured hosts with ports never match

The host validator accepts entries such as `example.com:8080`, but `URI#host` returns only `example.com`, so this query cannot match that stored entry. Conversely, an entry without a port matches requests on any port. Compare normalized authorities consistently or remove port support from validation if ports are intentionally ignored.

Legacy allowed hosts are not migrated

`cmd_tuples` reports rows affected by commands such as INSERT or UPDATE; for this SELECT it is zero, even when rows were returned. Consequently, the migration skips the host import and then deletes the legacy `embeddable_hosts` setting on line 31, losing the configured allowlist and disabling existing embeds. Check the result's row count instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no topic-user row

`TopicUser.find_by` returns `nil` for users who have not yet created a `TopicUser` record for this topic, but the next line dereferences `tu.notification_level`. Such users receive an error instead of being unsubscribed. Handle the missing row by creating a muted preference (or use the model's change helper).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
A GET request changes the logged-in user's notification preference

The unsubscribe URL is a GET endpoint that mutates the current user's topic preference without a confirmation or signed per-user token. A cross-site link or embedded resource can therefore cause a logged-in user to mute a topic, and email link scanners that fetch the URL can trigger the change before the user clicks it. Avoid state changes on ordinary GET requests or require an explicit, protected confirmation.

Saving the preference directly bypasses TopicUser change handling

Calling `save!` here bypasses `TopicUser.change`, which records `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` and publishes the notification-level change. In particular, if the reason remains `nil`, `TopicUser.update_last_read` can later auto-promote this preference to tracking, undoing the unsubscribe. Use the shared change path and set the reason as a user change.

The unsubscribe action can resubscribe users and does not always mute

This endpoint toggles notification state rather than applying an unsubscribe. A second visit changes a muted topic back to regular, so refreshing or reopening the email link reverses the user's choice. Also, a watching or tracking topic is only downgraded to regular, which does not mute it. Make the operation idempotently set the topic to muted.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent matches can lose statistics increments

The method reads `match_count`, increments it in Ruby, and saves the whole record. If two signup validations match the same blocked address concurrently, both can read the same count and write the same incremented value, so one match is lost. Use an atomic database increment (and update `last_match_at` atomically) if these statistics are expected to be accurate.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked addresses can be bypassed by changing letter case

This lookup compares the submitted email to the stored address exactly, but email domains are case-insensitive and the application otherwise normalizes email addresses for lookup. If `blocked@example.com` is listed, a user can sign up with `blocked@EXAMPLE.COM` and avoid the block. Normalize both the stored address and lookup value, or make the comparison case-insensitive.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Imported HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization

This marks imported content as `raw_html`, and the embed view renders `post.cooked` as raw HTML. RSS item content is external input, so a feed entry can include script or other executable markup that will be stored and run for forum visitors. The generated “Imported from” link also interpolates the feed item URL into HTML without escaping. Sanitize the content and escape generated attributes before storing it as raw HTML.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Standard RSS items without `content` abort the feed poll

This assumes every item has a non-nil `content` field, but ordinary RSS items commonly provide their body in `description` instead. Calling `scrub` on nil raises, aborting the poll; because retries are disabled, the remaining items are not imported during that run. Fall back to the available description/content field and handle items with neither.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
A crash between setting and expiring the throttle key can block retrieval permanently

The Redis key is created with `SETNX` and only then given a 60-second expiry. If the worker exits between these commands, the key remains without a TTL, so future retrievals for this URL are throttled indefinitely (except for staff bypasses). Set the key and expiry atomically.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex layout disables the small-action button's right float

Making `.small-action` a flex container causes its direct `button` child to become a flex item, so the existing `float: right` on that button no longer positions it at the far right. When the description does not fill the row, the button will sit immediately after the description instead of remaining right-aligned, changing the small-action layout.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

false_positives.candidate:
The new website name bypasses the untrusted-website restriction

`website` is gated by `untrusted_attributes`, which hides it from anonymous viewers for TL0 users, but `website_name` is added as an ordinary attribute and is computed directly from that hidden website. As a result, anonymous viewers can still learn the website host—and, when it matches the instance domain, its full path—even though the serializer intentionally withholds the website URL. Apply the same visibility check to `website_name` or omit it whenever `website` is restricted.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the last member on a page can leave the list empty

The offset is clamped to `user_count`, but an offset equal to the new count is past the last member. If a user removes the only member on the final page, the reload requests that offset and displays an empty page even though earlier members remain. Clamp to the start of the last valid page when the count decreases.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exact page-size counts produce an extra page

Using `floor(user_count / limit) + 1` reports an extra page whenever the member count is an exact multiple of the page size. For example, 50 members at a limit of 50 shows page 1 of 2 and enables Next, which loads an empty page. Use a ceiling-based page count.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

false_positives.candidate:
Changing the site locale can leave cached fallback translations stale

The fallback chain depends on the mutable `SiteSetting.default_locale`, but the translation cache is keyed only by translation key and current locale. After the site default locale changes, cached translations that came from the old fallback locale can continue to be returned until evicted or the cache is reset, so users may see translations from the previous setting.

Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests

This is the only call that ensures the fallback locale files are loaded, but translations are also looked up outside controller requests—for example in mailers and background jobs. The translation accelerator loads only the requested locale on its own, so a missing key in those contexts cannot be found in the site-default or English files and falls through as a missing translation.

Do not disable conditional passkeys when no user is selected

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offsets cause Django queryset slicing to raise

When advanced pagination is enabled and a cursor has a negative offset, this code passes that offset directly to a Django `QuerySet` slice. Django does not support negative queryset indices and raises an exception rather than interpreting them as reverse pagination, so a negative cursor sent to the optimized endpoint produces a server error. Use a supported query strategy or reject negative offsets.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Datetime audit-log ordering fails in the optimized paginator

The audit-log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` to this paginator, but `datetime` fields cannot be passed to `math.floor` or `math.ceil`. On any non-empty optimized page, cursor construction calls `get_item_key` and raises `TypeError`, so authorized requests with `optimized_pagination=true` fail instead of returning results. This paginator needs datetime-aware key conversion, like `DateTimePaginator`.

Negative offsets are rejected by Django queryset slicing

Optimized paginator cannot paginate datetime fields

This implementation assumes the ordering key is numeric, but the audit-log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`. `math.floor()` cannot accept a `datetime`, so building cursors for non-empty results raises `TypeError`; the corresponding cursor value conversion also returns an integer instead of a datetime. false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Eviction can remove the segment root

The size cap evicts members solely by their end-timestamp score. If the root span has an earlier score than the 1,000 retained spans, `zpopmin` removes it while the root marker remains set. The buffer will then flush the remaining spans using the root span ID as their segment ID, but without emitting the root payload, producing an incomplete and misleading segment.

Existing Redis sets are incompatible with the new sorted-set commands

This changes buffer keys from Redis sets to sorted sets, but existing keys written by the previous version remain alive until their TTL expires. During a rolling deploy, `zadd` on one of those set keys raises `WRONGTYPE`; the Lua script also now uses sorted-set commands on keys that may still be sets. Processing can therefore fail for up to the buffer TTL after deployment. Use a migration/versioned key scheme or handle old keys before switching types.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check the dataset actually being queried

This passes the endpoint’s original `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`. Dashboard widget splitting can call `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` for an error-only query while the original dataset is a metrics dataset; the eligibility helper then rejects upsampling for that metrics dataset, so the split error count is returned unadjusted even when all projects are allowlisted. Pass the scoped dataset so eligibility matches the query being executed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
Substring matching misidentifies error-focused queries

Checking for `event.type:error` anywhere in the raw query does not establish that the query selects error events. For example, `!event.type:error` contains this substring but selects non-error events, so an allowlisted Discover query can replace `count()` with `sum(sample_weight)` for transactions and return incorrect counts. Conversely, error-only queries expressed as `!event.type:transaction` are not recognized, so their counts are not upsampled. Determine the effective event-type filter from parsed query conditions rather than a substring check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The new table visualization receives no query results

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, this branch passes `columns: []` and an empty `tableData` instead of the current `result`'s fields, metadata, and rows. Dashboard table widgets therefore render blank for organizations using the new visualization, even when the query returned data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-valued age or timestamp bypasses mutual-exclusion validation

These validators use truthiness to check whether the other field was supplied. Since `timestamp=0` and `age=0` are valid values, a report containing both fields is accepted whenever the field checked by `get()` is zero. false_positives.candidate:
All replay errors are appended to every paginated segment result

The paginator invokes `on_results` for each page of recording segments, but this callback receives the complete replay's `error_events` list on every invocation. `gen_request_data` emits every error left after processing the page's segments, so errors are repeated across pages and summaries for a page can include errors outside that page's time range.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code redemption is not atomic

Two login requests can read the same backup-code list before either update completes. Both can validate the same code, then both write a list with that code nulled and both issue authenticated sessions. This makes a supposedly single-use recovery code reusable under concurrent requests. Consume the code with an atomic conditional update or equivalent serialization, and reject the request if another redemption already changed the list.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code authentication is not tested

The added test only checks that backup codes can be displayed, copied, and downloaded; it never redeems one during login or verifies that a redeemed code is rejected on reuse. Those are the core authentication and single-use guarantees of this feature, so regressions in the new credential-validation and persistence path can pass the suite unnoticed.

OAuth 2FA login has no backup-code option

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.

Create CalDAV events in the calendar belonging to the current host

Secondary hosts' credentials consequently try to create the event at the first host's calendar URL; that URL may be inaccessible with their credentials, so their calendar event is not created. Delete legacy Google events from their configured destination calendar

If a reference has no `externalCalendarId`, this lookup searches for a destination with an undefined external ID and returns no calendar. The subsequent fallback is `primary`, even when the event was created on a configured non-primary destination calendar. Google returns 404 for that deletion, which this method treats as success, leaving the event orphaned in the calendar.

Do not use the first host's calendar for every Lark credential

Each collective host's Lark service receives the full destination-calendar array, but this selects only its first entry. A secondary host's credential is therefore used against the first host's calendar ID, which can fail authorization or put the event in the wrong calendar. Select the destination belonging to the current credential.

Fall back to the destination calendar when updating legacy references

When `externalCalendarId` is absent, this searches for a destination whose `externalId` is also absent, so it returns `undefined` rather than the configured destination calendar. Updates for bookings with legacy references that lack an external calendar ID are then sent without a valid Google `calendarId` and fail. Select the destination calendar for the current host credential

Collective bookings pass the full destination-calendar array to each host's calendar service, but this always selects element zero. For every secondary Office 365 host, the request then targets the first host's calendar ID using the secondary host's access token. The request fails or creates the event in the wrong calendar, leaving those hosts without the booking. Select the destination associated with the current credential instead.

Use the current host's destination email in the Google attendee list

The Google event is inserted into the calendar selected by `credentialId`, but the organizer attendee email is always taken from the first destination calendar. For a secondary host's event, this identifies the first host as the organizer instead of the host whose calendar is being used, so the event can be attributed to or invite the wrong host. true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The sync token schema strips required token fields

These computed keys are not wildcards: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the same literal key for both entries, so the second property overwrites the first. Zod also strips unrecognized object properties by default. In credential-sync mode, parsing therefore drops fields such as `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, and `refresh_token`; token refresh then stores stale or missing values, causing repeated refreshes or unusable credentials.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest email normalization lets callers bypass the blacklist

Blacklist entries are lowercased, but submitted guest addresses are compared without normalization. Because email validation does not lowercase addresses, a caller can submit a blacklisted address with different casing and have it inserted and sent invitations. Normalize both sides before checking; the same normalization should be used when detecting existing attendees.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team authorization requires users to be both admin and owner

The team permission check joins `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` with `&&`, so a team admin who is not also an owner is rejected. This prevents the team-admin role from using the endpoint even though the booking UI treats admins and owners as authorized. Use an OR between the role checks.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add-guest notifications ignore event-type email-disable settings

Unlike the other booking email senders, this function does not check the event type's `disableStandardEmails` settings. Adding guests therefore sends host and attendee notifications even when standard emails are disabled for that event type, defeating the configured preference. Apply the host and attendee disable checks here as well.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
A calendar sync failure leaves guests inserted but prevents notifications

The database attendee update has already committed before this external calendar update runs. If the update throws, the mutation fails before sending any emails, but the guests remain in the database; retrying those addresses then finds no new guests and errors. The operation can therefore leave guests added without calendar updates or invitations, with no way to recover through the same request. Handle this partial-failure case, for example by making retries idempotent and ensuring notifications/sync can be retried.

The endpoint allows guests to be added to cancelled bookings

The handler never checks the booking status, so an authorized attendee can call this mutation for a cancelled or rejected booking even though the UI only offers the action for confirmed bookings. The new attendee is then sent a scheduled email with a confirmed calendar invitation for an event that is no longer active. Reject bookings that are not in an eligible status on the server.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry increments can be lost when cron runs overlap

This writes a value derived from the reminder snapshot fetched earlier rather than atomically incrementing the database value. If two cron invocations process the same failed reminder concurrently, both can read `retryCount = 0` and write `1`; repeated overlaps can prevent the count from reaching the `gt: 1` cleanup threshold, so persistently failing reminders are not reliably deleted after two failures. Use an atomic increment (and consider preventing concurrent processing of the same reminder).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Removing `findMany` breaks the service query API

This replaces the public `findMany` method with `getBaseConditions`, which only returns a SQL condition and does not execute a query or accept the previous selection and caller-supplied filters. Existing callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` will fail to compile (or fail at runtime if they are not type-checked), and there is no equivalent query method in this class. Preserve the method or migrate all callers as part of this change.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Use a portable in-place sed invocation

`sed -i ''` is the macOS form of in-place editing and fails on GNU sed, commonly used by Linux developers. When `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` already exists, the script therefore fails to replace it; because the script does not stop on errors, it can still print that the environment file was updated. Use a portable invocation or detect the platform.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Expired cache rows are reported as active cache status

This aggregation includes cache rows regardless of `expiresAt`, but cache reads only serve rows whose expiry is still in the future. Since expired rows can remain in the table, a credential with no usable cache can still get a `cacheUpdatedAt` value and appear to have cached data in the UI. Filter the status query to unexpired rows if this status is meant to describe available cache data.

Invalidate calendar data after deleting the cache

The delete mutation reports success but does not invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. That query supplies `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to show the old cache status and delete action after the cache has been removed unless the optional `onSuccess` callback happens to refresh it or the page is reloaded. Invalidate the query on success, as the disconnect mutation already does.

`ENV_FILE` is relative to the caller's working directory, not this script. Running the usual `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` from the repository root points to `../.env` outside the repository, so the script creates or updates the wrong file and the app does not receive the configured webhook URL. Resolve the path from the script location or repository root.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

Immediate email cancellations still consume SendGrid’s cancellation limit

This branch posts `status: "cancel"` directly to SendGrid instead of marking the reminder for the cron job. SendGrid keeps these cancelled scheduled sends until their scheduled dates, so workflow deletions, step deletions, and reschedules can still accumulate pending cancellations and hit the 100-cancellation limit this change is intended to avoid. For rescheduled bookings, this branch also leaves the reminder row in the database without setting `cancelled`, so the cron job will not process it.

This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

false_positives.candidate:
A reminder can send before the periodic cancellation job runs

Cancelled reminders are only sent to SendGrid for cancellation when this cron endpoint runs. With a 15-minute cron interval, a reminder scheduled less than 15 minutes away can be sent before the next run processes it, even though its booking was already cancelled or rescheduled. This leaves a window where the original reminder is still delivered.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring cancellation no longer waits for calendar deletions

This `forEach` callback now suspends at `await getCalendar`, but `forEach` does not wait for async callbacks. The handler can reach `Promise.all(apiDeletes)` at line 652 while `apiDeletes` is still empty, then return success before any recurring calendar events are deleted. If the process exits or the import/deletion fails, the external events remain even though the bookings are cancelled.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
All app imports start eagerly when the store is loaded

Each `import()` is executed while this object is constructed, so loading the app-store module immediately starts imports for every integration, even when the caller needs only one app. Since common paths import the store, this still loads all provider modules and incurs their startup and memory costs rather than loading only the requested app.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours validation can accept unavailable slots and reject valid ones

This only returns a match when a same-day interval fails the bounds check. If the host has no interval for that weekday, `.find` returns nothing and the slot is accepted; if the host has multiple intervals that day, a slot inside one can be rejected because it falls outside another. It also compares only the slot start time, so an event can extend past the host’s availability end. In round-robin availability assembled from other hosts, this can expose slots the fixed host cannot take.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length date overrides are never recognized as equal

This compares two Dayjs objects with `===`, which tests object identity rather than whether their timestamps match. For a zero-length override, the intended equality case is skipped; the subsequent range checks can then incorrectly allow a slot that spans that timestamp instead of treating the override as unavailable.

false_positives.candidate:
Date overrides bypass busy-time checks

When a slot falls within a date override, this returns `true` before checking `busy`. Date overrides add availability; they do not make existing bookings or calendar events disappear. A fixed host can therefore be shown as available during an existing booking or busy calendar event, allowing a conflicting round-robin booking.

OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

GitHub OAuth request failures escape the installation error flow

The token exchange and subsequent `get_user_info` call are outside any error handling. If GitHub rejects the code with an HTTP error, or the `/user` request fails (for example, a rejected token or transient API error), these calls can raise instead of returning the installation failure response. This produces an unhandled error rather than the failure screen promised for invalid or reused codes; catch the relevant request/API exceptions and route them through `error()`.

Installation proceeds without verifying the installer when no integration exists yet

When the installation record has not been created by the webhook yet, this branch advances the pipeline without checking the authenticated GitHub user. The next step can create the integration, so a callback racing ahead of webhook processing bypasses the installer-identity check entirely. Verify the sender through a reliable source before advancing, or fail/retry until that identity is available.

That stale value is included in the serialized task payload, making the queued time inaccurate for every later inbound assignment. false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). Metric alert handler is now uninstantiable

`StatefulDetectorHandler` is abstract and requires implementations of `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. This `pass` subclass implements none of them, so accessing `detector.detector_handler` for a detector with this group type raises `TypeError` instead of returning a handler. false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Return the normalized monitor config

`config` is copied and its `schedule_type` is replaced with the display value above, but the context returns `monitor.config` instead. As a result, occurrence monitor context exposes the raw schedule type rather than the intended display value, and the normalization is discarded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
A join timeout can leave later flusher processes running

When the deadline expires while waiting for one process, this `break` skips the remaining processes, including their `terminate()` calls. Any skipped worker blocked in a producer operation can remain alive after the consumer has shut down and may continue producing alongside a replacement consumer. Ensure every worker is stopped even after the shared join deadline expires.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Negative process limits crash flusher initialization

The `--flusher-processes` option accepts any integer, but a negative value makes `num_processes` negative and creates an empty `process_to_shards_map`. With assigned shards, the distribution loop then computes an index and looks it up in that empty map, raising `KeyError` while the consumer starts. Validate the option as positive or reject invalid values before building the map.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed work is marked complete and can be committed

The `finally` block marks every work item complete, including items whose `result_processor` raised an exception. The commit loop can then advance past a message whose processing failed, permanently losing its result. Only mark the offset complete after successful processing, or preserve the failure so it can be retried.

Offset gaps can permanently block commits

This tracker requires every integer offset between the last committed offset and the next completed message to appear in `all_offsets`. Kafka can legitimately deliver messages with gaps in offsets, for example because of compaction or aborted transactions; those missing offsets will never be submitted, so commits stop advancing and tracked offsets accumulate indefinitely. Track the order of delivered messages rather than requiring contiguous integer offsets.

Shutdown exits workers without draining queued work

Setting `worker.shutdown` makes the loop exit after the current item, even though `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is intended to let the queue drain. Any remaining queued messages are abandoned without being processed or committed, so shutdown causes those messages to be replayed and may duplicate side effects. Drain queued items before exiting, or explicitly account for them during shutdown.

The work queues are unbounded

`queue.Queue()` defaults to unlimited capacity, so a sustained input rate above worker throughput keeps accumulating work in memory instead of applying backpressure. Under overload this can grow until the consumer process runs out of memory; use bounded queues and handle the resulting backpressure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key components can collide

The key concatenates the resource name and parent folder with `_` but does not escape or length-prefix either component. For the same namespace, user, and action, `(name="foo_bar", parent="baz")` and `(name="foo", parent="bar_baz")` produce the same key. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny a different, permitted resource for the cache TTL.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached denials mask newly granted permissions

A denial is retained for the full cache TTL, and `Check` consults this cache before checking even a fresh permission map. If a user is denied and then granted access to that resource, every check with the same key continues to return denied until the denial entry expires, rather than using the database fallback to observe the grant. This regresses prompt visibility of newly created resources or permission changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable

The previous ability check detected federated groups through `source_tenants` and disabled editing and deletion for their rules. This refactor hard-codes `isFederated` to `false`, so federated rules can now appear editable or deletable whenever the user has the corresponding permissions. Attempts to mutate these rules can fail or violate the federated-rule restrictions; preserve the group’s federated status in the ability check.

Pause is unavailable for Prometheus-only Grafana rules

The new list path supplies only `promRule`, but this menu item is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. The rule detail link drops the return-to location

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

If the count is one below the limit, concurrent requests for different devices can both observe capacity and both insert, leaving the active device count above the configured limit. true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. When the limit is reached, that write fails but the cache entry remains; on the next request, the cache-hit path returns nil without checking the store, so `Authenticate` grants the anonymous identity. true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Building large ID lists repeatedly copies the growing string

For SQLite batches above the parameter limit, each iteration formats a new string containing the entire list accumulated so far. This is quadratic in the number of IDs and can copy hundreds of megabytes for a batch of tens of thousands, making the large-batch cleanup path—and the added large-batch integration test—needlessly slow and allocation-heavy. Build the list with a builder or join formatted values once.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete metrics use object names as the kind label

This call passes `name` where the other storage-duration calls pass the resource kind. If this argument supplies the metric's kind label, each deleted object creates a distinct label value, causing unbounded Prometheus time-series cardinality and making the delete metrics inconsistent with other operations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation

The timeout context is derived from the incoming request context, so it is canceled as soon as the API request completes; the 10-second timeout does not detach it from that cancellation. Since these legacy writes run after the unified write returns, a client disconnect or normal request completion can cancel them before they finish. The same pattern is used for update, delete, and delete-collection, so successful unified writes can routinely fail to reach legacy storage.

Concurrent writes to one resource can reach legacy out of order

Each mutation launches an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. If a create, update, and delete for the same object are handled in quick succession, the legacy calls can execute in a different order; for example, a delayed create can run after a delete and leave a deleted object in legacy storage. This can make legacy reads disagree with unified storage even when every individual legacy call succeeds.

Legacy delete-collection results are recorded as storage metrics

This asynchronous call records the legacy operation with `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy delete-collection latency and failures are attributed to unified storage. The same instrumentation mix-up occurs when storage create or update fails, where `recordLegacyDuration` is called instead. Monitoring will therefore misreport which backend is slow or failing.

Legacy update recomputes the update against a different stored object

Passing the original UpdatedObjectInfo to the legacy store causes it to compute the update again using the legacy object as its base, rather than writing the object produced by the successful unified update. The stores can have different state or resource versions, so an update can fail in legacy or produce a different result there. This loses the prior behavior of forwarding the unified result and undermines the dual write's purpose of keeping the stores aligned.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock

Concurrent non-development calls can all observe an empty cache at lines 41–43 and then wait here. After the first call loads and caches the manifest, each waiter still proceeds to load it again because the cache is not rechecked under the lock. A burst of requests during startup therefore causes redundant manifest reads and cache replacements; recheck the cache after acquiring the lock and return it when populated.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent index builds can race with TotalDocs map iteration

`BuildIndex` now permits concurrent builds and writes to `b.cache` under `cacheMu`, but `TotalDocs` iterates the same map without taking that lock. If a build overlaps `TotalDocs`, Go can report a concurrent map iteration/write and crash the process. This can occur during startup if a watch event triggers an index build after the watch starts but before the initialization log calls `TotalDocs`. Protect the iteration with the same lock or otherwise snapshot the cache safely.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

false_positives.candidate:
Initialization failure returns without cleaning up initialized resources

`NewResourceServer` now runs `Init` before returning, but on an error it returns `nil` without stopping the lifecycle hooks or canceling the server context. If lifecycle initialization has opened resources, or search initialization has started its background watcher before a later initialization step fails, there is no returned server for the caller to stop and those resources can leak. Clean up partially initialized components before returning the error.

Starting the resource watcher after index initialization can drop events

`search.init` can take a long time, but the resource watcher is now started only after it completes. `WatchWriteEvents` begins polling from the latest resource version when it is opened, so writes made by other server instances during index construction are not replayed to this server's watch stream. Clients reconnecting with a `Since` version from before startup can therefore miss changes. Start the resource watcher before the long index build, or ensure the watcher replays from a durable cursor.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

As a result, none of the providers created by this test are removed; the same mistake is repeated at line 425. false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider, not Bouncy Castle

The provider contract promises a Bouncy Castle security provider, but this returns whichever provider implements the JVM's default keystore type (commonly SUN). Callers that use this method for Bouncy Castle services will receive the wrong provider and may fail or use unintended implementations.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding an abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public interface, and adding abstract order() breaks compatibility for third-party implementations compiled against the previous interface: provider discovery now invokes order() on them and can fail with AbstractMethodError. Make this a default method with a documented fallback priority, or otherwise preserve compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Reject ECDSA integers that exceed the fixed signature width

When a decoded DER INTEGER is wider than the expected ECDSA component, this code silently discards its most significant bytes. An oversized value can therefore map to the same fixed-width r or s as a valid signature, so malformed DER signatures are accepted as valid after conversion. Reject out-of-range integers instead of truncating them.

The selected global crypto provider leaves most crypto operations unsupported

AuthzClient.create initializes the process-wide CryptoIntegration, and this provider can be selected when the authz-client is used without another provider. The selected provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for most CryptoProvider methods, so unrelated Keycloak crypto operations in the same JVM then fail instead of using a complete provider. Implement or delegate the remaining operations, or avoid registering this partial implementation as the global provider.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Preserve MANAGE_CLIENTS access to client role mappings

These overrides check only the V2 permission and omit the `MANAGE_CLIENTS` role fallback provided by the existing client evaluator. As a result, administrators with the built-in `manage-clients` role can manage client configuration but are denied client-role mapping operations (and the same omission applies to the composite and client-scope mapping checks below). Preserve the existing role-based authorization when adding V2 permissions.

Provision the Clients schema for existing admin-permissions clients

The new Clients scopes and resource type are only written when `init` creates the admin-permissions client. `init` returns immediately when that client already exists, so realms upgraded with an existing V2 admin-permissions client retain only the old Users schema: the Clients resource and scopes are absent, and client permission creation/evaluation cannot work. Add an upgrade path that provisions missing schema elements for existing clients.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
View permission grants global group-management access

This check treats either `view` or `manage` on the all-groups resource as `canManage()`. Callers of the no-argument `requireManage()`—including top-level group creation—therefore allow an administrator with only view permission to perform management operations across the realm. Require the `manage` scope here; view permission must not grant write access.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group-scoped user search uses authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

`hasPermission` expects a group ID and resolves it with `findByName`, but this call passes `groupResource.getId()` (the authorization resource's database ID). As a result, individual group member-view permissions are not recognized here; line 123 also adds that resource ID to the set consumed as group IDs by user searches. Group-restricted searches can therefore return incomplete or empty pages because filtering happens after pagination without the intended group constraint.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor fails to reject a null raw token ID

The second null check checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`, so a context with a null raw ID is accepted. Encoding that context appends the literal string `null` to the token ID, producing an ID that does not preserve the supplied context and can be mistaken for a real raw ID. Check `rawTokenId` here.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token event matcher does not verify the grant shortcut

This matcher extracts characters 3–4 instead of the grant shortcut at characters 4–5, and returns false when the extracted value equals the expected shortcut. As a result, it does not reliably assert that an event token ID has the expected grant type, so regressions in grant-type encoding can pass these integration assertions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.

Decoder assumes every grant shortcut is exactly two characters

The decoder splits the context into fixed two-character fields and requires a six-character prefix, but `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` documents shortcuts as usually three letters and does not enforce a two-character limit. A custom grant using a three-character shortcut can therefore produce an ID during encoding that this decoder rejects or misinterprets, making the token context unreadable. Align the extension contract with the format or support variable-length shortcuts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes remain reusable in user storage

This validator only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list; it never removes or marks the matched code as used. Unlike the local recovery-code provider, this user-storage implementation therefore accepts the same recovery code on every login, defeating the one-time-use security guarantee. Consume the matched code and persist the updated list, and cover reuse with a test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The concurrency test does not wait for the reader thread

The test sets `deletedAll` and immediately asserts on `caughtExceptions` without joining the reader thread. The reader may still be handling an in-flight request, so an exception from the concurrent access can arrive after the assertion and the test can pass falsely; the thread can also continue using the realm after test teardown. Wait for the reader to terminate before asserting, and ensure it is stopped even if deletion fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
A join timeout can leave later flusher processes running

When the deadline expires while waiting for one process, this `break` skips the remaining processes, including their `terminate()` calls. Any skipped worker blocked in a producer operation can remain alive after the consumer has shut down and may continue producing alongside a replacement consumer. Ensure every worker is stopped even after the shared join deadline expires.

Negative process limits crash flusher initialization

The `--flusher-processes` option accepts any integer, but a negative value makes `num_processes` negative and creates an empty `process_to_shards_map`. With assigned shards, the distribution loop then computes an index and looks it up in that empty map, raising `KeyError` while the consumer starts. false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

Zero-valued age or timestamp bypasses mutual-exclusion validation

Since `timestamp=0` and `age=0` are valid values, a report containing both fields is accepted whenever the field checked by `get()` is zero. Check field presence instead so the endpoint consistently rejects reports containing both.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: using `.get()` and truthiness to check for the presence of `timestamp` and `age` allows a value of `0` to be treated as absent, thus bypassing the mutual-exclusion validation. Both suggest checking for field presence instead.

Failed work is marked complete and can be committed

The work queues are unbounded

Shutdown exits workers without draining queued work

Since these legacy writes run after the unified write returns, a client disconnect or normal request completion can cancel them before they finish. The same pattern is used for update, delete, and delete-collection, so successful unified writes can routinely fail to reach legacy storage.

Legacy update recomputes the update against a different stored object

Passing the original UpdatedObjectInfo to the legacy store causes it to compute the update again using the legacy object as its base, rather than writing the object produced by the successful unified update. The stores can have different state or resource versions, so an update can fail in legacy or produce a different result there. This loses the prior behavior of forwarding the unified result and undermines the dual write's purpose of keeping the stores aligned.

Concurrent writes to one resource can reach legacy out of order

Each mutation launches an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. If a create, update, and delete for the same object are handled in quick succession, the legacy calls can execute in a different order; for example, a delayed create can run after a delete and leave a deleted object in legacy storage. This can make legacy reads disagree with unified storage even when every individual legacy call succeeds.

Legacy delete-collection results are recorded as storage metrics

This asynchronous call records the legacy operation with `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy delete-collection latency and failures are attributed to unified storage. The same instrumentation mix-up occurs when storage create or update fails, where `recordLegacyDuration` is called instead. Monitoring will therefore misreport which backend is slow or failing.

A cross-site link or embedded resource can therefore cause a logged-in user to mute a topic, and email link scanners that fetch the URL can trigger the change before the user clicks it.
